source: Polya (1945) How to Solve It, as summarised in Lee et al. (2026)
finding: Polya proposed four phases: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back. Heuristics (specialise, generalise, work backwards, analogy, auxiliary problem) serve the planning phase.
numbers: Four phases. No experiment in the book. Read here only as a second-hand description in the Llama-Polya paper.
limits: The book itself was not opened. It is descriptive, not a tested model; it gives no rule for when to pick a heuristic.
agent_relevance: Maps to our S-states: restate (understand), operator choice (plan), execute, verify (look back). The phases are a checklist, not a controller.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving, as described in Schoenfeld (1982) and Rott (2013)
finding: Schoenfeld's framework has four parts: resources (knowledge), heuristics, control (monitoring and resource management) and belief systems. Success depends on all four, and control is the part Polya left out.
numbers: Four categories. Episodes: reading, analysis, exploration, planning/implementation, verification.
limits: Read via the 1982 paper and Rott's 2013 paper, not the 1985 book. I did not read the 1985 tables.
agent_relevance: Direct design source for our control layer (S6) and for keeping resources, heuristics and control in separate code paths.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) Beyond the Purely Cognitive: Metacognition and Social Cognition as Driving Forces in Intellectual Performance
finding: Compares recorded protocols. Two students (protocol 1) pick a direction on a geometry construction problem, calculate until the 20-minute tape runs out and cannot say what the answer would be good for. An expert starts with less relevant knowledge, raises about a dozen possible wild goose chases and drops each after brief thought, then solves a problem the students failed.
numbers: Qualitative: 3 protocols (two student pairs, one mathematician). In protocol 1 the pair spent 2.5 min, then 5 min, on empirical work for one conjecture. 20-minute tape ran out during calculation.
quote: one bad decision, unmonitored and unchecked, dooms an entire solution to failure
limits: Case studies, no inferential statistics, small N. Chosen as typical, not sampled. Schoenfeld notes recording students in pairs changed behaviour compared with solo work.
agent_relevance: The failure was a control failure, not a knowledge failure. Argues for a code-side monitor that cuts a branch with no progress, which fits G1 (doubt on signal) and the impasse detector.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) knowledge-belief-value framework
finding: Schoenfeld sets out a cross product of settings (self, cognitive structures, environment) and knowledge/belief/value systems, with degrees of awareness: unaware, aware but non-reflective, locally aware and reflective, reflexive abstraction. Beliefs about the task shape which heuristics are even tried.
numbers: Qualitative framework. Example: students believed a sketched helper circle did not belong in a 'proper' figure and erased it.
limits: Not tested as a model. The awareness levels are a taxonomy, not measured scales.
agent_relevance: Beliefs are mirrored in an LLM by its prior about what a good answer looks like. A schema can override this with checks on output, not with instructions.

source: Schoenfeld (1979) Explicit heuristic training as a variable in problem-solving performance
finding: ERIC abstract: seven upper-division college students were studied in detail while working problems solvable with one or more heuristics. Explicit heuristic training was the variable.
numbers: ERIC abstract gives N = 7 and nothing more. I did not read the paper, so I give no effect numbers.
limits: Abstract only. Very small N. No scores in the record.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that heuristics can be taught; no transfer numbers available here.

source: Schoenfeld (1980) Teaching problem-solving skills
finding: ERIC abstract: explores whether students can be taught to recognise and apply the problem-solving strategies experts use.
numbers: Abstract only, no numbers.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Says the strategy-library approach is teachable by humans; says nothing about LLMs.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) as quoted by Rott (2013): wild goose chase before and after a metacognitive course
finding: About 60% of university students showed 'wild goose chase' behaviour: pick a direction and push it until time runs out, with no reflection. After a course where the teacher kept asking three questions, the share not regulating fell to 20%, with a matching rise in success.
numbers: 60% down to 20% (as quoted). No N in the quote.
quote: What exactly are you doing? Why are you doing it? How does it help you?
limits: Second-hand quote from Rott. I did not open Schoenfeld 1992 itself. One teacher's classes; no control group stated.
agent_relevance: Three cheap questions (what are you doing, why, does it help) could be a code-triggered check. Must still follow G1: fire on a signal, not on a timer.

source: Rott (2013) Process regulation in the problem-solving processes of fifth graders
finding: Tests with Grade 5 pupils whether Schoenfeld's wild goose chase finding, made at Grade 7 and university level, holds below Grade 7. Processes coded in Schoenfeld's episode scheme. A process made only of analysis and exploration episodes counted as a wild goose chase. It strongly predicted failure.
numbers: 88 processes. 32 wild goose chase: 27 reached only none/basic access, 5 reached advanced/full. 56 others: 16 none/basic, 40 advanced/full. Chi-square 25.378, p < 0.0001. 10 of 19 'Squares on a Chessboard' processes excluded. 45 children in four groups.
limits: Small sample forced merging outcome classes into two. Wild goose chase is defined by missing planning/verifying, so part of the link to success is built in. Few tasks.
agent_relevance: Cheap detectable signal: a run with only explore/analyse steps and no plan or check step. Countable in code from the operator log.

source: Rott (2013) junctures between episodes
finding: About 25% of processes were also coded with a second scheme (Cohors-Fresenborg and Kaune). In almost all cases the junctures between episodes carried metacognitive activity, mostly focus of attention and reflective checks.
numbers: About 25% of processes double-coded; 'almost all' junctures had metacognition (no exact count in the text I read).
quote: where managerial decisions (or their absence) will make or break a solution
limits: Double-coded subset only; agreement figure not captured.
agent_relevance: Supports putting control decisions at transitions between operators, not inside them.

source: Lester, Garofalo and Kroll (1989) as quoted in Rott (2013)
finding: In two Grade 7 classes, the more successful solvers were better at monitoring and regulating their activity than the poorer ones.
numbers: Two classes. No scores in the quote.
limits: Second-hand quote. Correlational; monitoring skill and maths knowledge are confounded.
agent_relevance: Monitoring correlates with success in children as in adults. Consistent with S6 but not causal evidence.

source: Mevarech and Kramarski (1997) IMPROVE, as cited in Rott (2013)
finding: Rott cites this as a Grade 7 study of the impact of metacognitive questioning on maths problem solving. I did not read it.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the citation context was read.
agent_relevance: Suggests metacognitive question prompts help; check the original before using any number.

source: Kuzle (2019) Design and evaluation of materials for the working backward strategy
finding: 14 Grade 5 students got explicit heuristic training for about one school year (WoBa). Before training almost all used working backward intuitively but struggled with complex reversing tasks. After training results improved considerably and every student used the strategy in the post-test.
numbers: N = 14. Pre-test and post-test each 3 tasks. On one bridge-crossing task, 8 students were at the two lowest backward levels before training. After training 10 solved a task partly (WB3) or fully (WB4). 2 students were fully right (WB4) both before and after. Working backward improved in 7 of the other 12.
limits: No control group; design-based research. Interested volunteers. Post-test content did not match the previous year's curriculum, which hurt results. Tiny sample.
agent_relevance: Working backward is easy to try but hard to execute on multi-step chains, as with models (see RevThink, FOBAR). Use it as a verifier operator, not the main solver.

source: Asmus (2010) and Amit and Portnov-Neeman (2016) as reviewed in Kuzle (2019)
finding: Reversal is not present from the start. In Grade 2 classes no control-group child solved a problem with an unknown initial state, but at least 9% of potentially gifted Grade 2 students did. In Grade 4, 36% reached the correct solution. Explicit training of working backward helped talented Grade 6 students over a control group.
numbers: Grade 2 gifted N = 182: at least 9% correct, 35% reasonable approach. Grade 4: 36% correct. Grade 6: trained group above control (no figures quoted).
limits: Second-hand summaries. Gifted samples. Word problems with an unknown start state were much harder than symbolic ones.
agent_relevance: Unknown-start-state problems are the hard ones; the trap is reversing every operation in the right order.

source: Lee et al. (2026) Llama-Polya: instruction tuning based on Polya's problem solving
finding: Llama-3.1-8B was fine-tuned on synthetic GSM8K tutoring dialogues in Polya's four stages. Variants compared: base, instruct, metamath, polya-v2, metamath then polya-v2. Models tuned on maths data (polya-v2, metamath) had the most balanced stage mix and lowest error rates. Base and instruct models often skipped stages and gave the answer early.
numbers: Error rates: polya-v2 0.0%, metamath 0.4%. Combined metamath+polya-v2 had high error rates. Dialogues of 10-20 turns across arithmetic, measurement and geometry. Six maths-education experts: self-level feedback 4.22/5, task-level feedback about 2.8 to 3.2.
limits: Small manual evaluation by the authors. 'Error' is stage-conformity error, not solving accuracy. No benchmark accuracy in what I read. The sequential-tuning conflict is unexplained.
agent_relevance: Polya stages are easy to impose as dialogue structure. This is a tutoring study, not a test that stages raise correct answers. Not evidence for an accuracy boost.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction
finding: Step-back prompting first asks for the principle or concept behind the question, then solves with it. This is generalising before solving. It lifts PaLM-2L on physics, chemistry, time-sensitive QA and multi-hop QA.
numbers: MMLU Physics: PaLM-2L 66.4% to 73.2% with step-back (CoT 65%). Chemistry: 70.9% to 81.8% (CoT 75.3%). GPT-4 physics 69.4% base, 82.9% CoT, 84.5% step-back; chemistry 80.9, 85.3, 85.6. Llama2-70B physics 51.9% to 64.8%, chemistry 55.7% to 66.7%. TimeQA 41.5% to 66%; with RAG 68.7%. 5 runs, SDs reported.
limits: Little or no edge over strong CoT on GPT-4 (84.5 vs 82.9; 85.6 vs 85.3). Tested on knowledge-heavy tasks, not pure maths.
agent_relevance: Generalise-first helps most where the failure is a wrong principle or recall step. One extra call.

source: Zheng et al. step-back: GSM8K and error analysis
finding: On GSM8K step-back is no better than simple baselines. On MMLU physics it fixes some errors and adds others. Reasoning, not abstraction, is the main remaining error source.
numbers: GSM8K PaLM-2L 75.8%, 1-shot 84.5%, zero-shot CoT 84.4%, step-back 84.3%. MMLU physics: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9% new ones. TimeQA: fixes 39.9% of baseline errors, causes 5.6%; step-back+RAG fixes 21.6% of RAG errors. In TimeQA remaining errors, 45% are retrieval failures.
limits: Authors' explanation for GSM8K (principles too simple) is untested.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: skip generalisation on easy arithmetic. Gate it in code by difficulty, since 11.9% new errors is real harm.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting
finding: Decompose a problem into easier subproblems, solve in order, reuse earlier answers. This is the specialise/simplify heuristic as a prompt. Large gain on compositional and length generalisation.
numbers: Last-letter concatenation (code-davinci-002): CoT 84.2/69.2/50.2/39.8/31.8 at list length 4/6/8/10/12; least-to-most 94.0/88.4/83.0/76.4/74.0. Standard prompting 0. SCAN length split: least-to-most 99.7% vs CoT 16.2% (standard 16.7%); text-davinci-002 76.0 vs 0.0; code-davinci-001 60.7.
limits: SCAN is synthetic and the 14 exemplars were tailored to it. Decomposition prompts were hand-built per task; the model did not discover them. 13 failures on SCAN length split.
agent_relevance: Easy-to-hard generalisation depends on the decomposition being right. Code can hold and check the subproblem list.

source: Zhou et al. least-to-most on GSM8K and DROP
finding: On real maths word problems the gain is small. It shows mainly on long chains.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT 60.87 vs least-to-most 62.39 (prose says 60.97). Problems needing 5+ steps: 39.07% to 45.23%. DROP non-football 74.77 to 82.45, football 59.56 to 73.42. Zero-shot 16.38, standard 17.06 on GSM8K. Nearly all GSM8K failures were solvable with a hand-crafted decomposition.
limits: Small average gain. Authors' explanation: most DROP problems are trivially decomposable. Prose and table differ slightly (60.97 vs 60.87).
agent_relevance: Decomposition quality is the bottleneck, not execution. Failure points to checking the plan, not the arithmetic.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting
finding: Zero-shot 'devise a plan, then carry it out' prompt (Polya phases 2 and 3). More detail (extract variables, compute intermediate results) gives PS+. Built after an error analysis of 46 GSM8K problems that zero-shot CoT got wrong.
numbers: Error analysis: 7% calculation errors, 27% missing-step errors, 27% semantic misunderstanding. PS+ beats zero-shot CoT by at least 5% on every arithmetic set except GSM8K (+2.9%); PS alone averages +2.5%. Roughly 8-shot CoT level on arithmetic. GPT-3 text-davinci-003. Zero-shot CoT with SC: 70.7% GSM8K, 81.7% SVAMP; PS+ with SC higher.
limits: Error percentages from a 46-problem sample. Older model. Prompt wording tuned on these datasets.
agent_relevance: Planning prompts fix omitted steps, not arithmetic slips. Pair with a code-side calculator for the 7% slice.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Model writes its own related problems and solutions, then solves the target (Polya's 'do you know a related problem?'). Beats 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench.
numbers: Average gain of +4% across tasks (abstract). MATH and GSM8K table cells were not cleanly extractable, so not recorded. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k and GPT-4; Acc@1 and Acc@10 reported.
limits: Exact table numbers not read cleanly. Self-generated examples can be wrong; I saw no check of their correctness.
agent_relevance: The related-problem heuristic works without hand-written examples. Self-written exemplars are model-correlated, so G4 applies.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover
finding: Model selects from seed reasoning modules (e.g. break into subtasks, critical thinking), adapts them and composes a task-level structure, then applies it. Decomposition and step-back type modules are among the seeds.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: BBH 56% base, 60% CoT, 61% plan-and-solve, 67% Self-Discover; T4D 30/40/42/69; MATH 45/42/49/50.5. GPT-4: BBH 58/75/73/81; T4D 51/52/53/85; MATH 70.5/71/70/73. Up to 32% over CoT; beats CoT-SC by over 20% with 10-40x less inference compute. MATH subset is 200 sampled problems.
limits: MATH gain over CoT only 3 to 8 points on PaLM and 2 on GPT-4 on a 200-problem sample. Biggest gains on agent and algorithmic tasks, not maths. Paper says many MATH failures are computation errors.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice helps less in maths where errors are calculation. Supports a code-side calculator.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse thinking makes LLMs stronger reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Teacher model writes forward reasoning, a backward question and backward reasoning. Student is trained on three tasks: forward reasoning, generate backward question, backward reasoning. Working backward is a training signal and consistency check.
numbers: 12 datasets: average +13.53% over student zero-shot and +6.84% over strongest distillation baselines. On 8 held-in sets: Mistral-7B +12.68%, Gemma-7B +14.37% (Mistral zero-shot avg 50.55); +6.44% to 7.15% over SKD and Distill Step-by-Step. With 10% of correct forward chains it beats standard fine-tuning on 10x more data (StrategyQA). Teacher Gemini-1.5-Pro; LoRA rank 32.
limits: A training method, not a prompt. Training on backward questions alone hurts, sometimes below zero-shot. MATH for the 7B student is only around 10 to 15%. Maths gain smaller than commonsense and tabular.
agent_relevance: Backward data teaches consistency but training is outside our scope. Warning: backward-only reasoning can harm.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) FOBAR: forward-backward reasoning for mathematical verification
finding: Mask one number in the question and ask the model to recover it given a candidate answer (a backward check). Combine the forward vote with the backward verification probability. A mechanical form of working backward from the answer.
numbers: Six maths sets (AddSub, MultiArith, SingleEQ, SVAMP, GSM8K, AQuA), three LLMs (text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4). FOBAR with ComplexCoT has highest average on all three. FOBAR beats Self-Consistency most of the time and Self-Verification on almost all sets. In one block of the table the averages read CoT 76.6, Self-Verification 75.8, FOBAR 83.5 (rows partly garbled in extraction).
limits: Template needs a number to mask, so it does not cover proofs or non-numeric answers. Table rows garbled in PDF text; per-model numbers uncertain. Paper states more sampled chains alone saturate.
agent_relevance: Best concrete evidence for a 'check by working backward' operator. Code builds the masked question, so no model judge is needed. Fits G3 (a pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Brown and Walter, The Art of Problem Posing (background)
finding: Teaches 'What-if-not': list the attributes of a problem, negate each, and pose new problems. Extends heuristics from solving to posing.
numbers: No numbers; a method book.
limits: Not opened. Described from general knowledge; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Systematic attribute variation could drive a code-run variation operator for stress tests.

source: Newell and Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving (background)
finding: Founded the problem-space view and means-ends analysis; Polya and Schoenfeld heuristics are the informal counterpart. Covered in subfields 01 and 02 of this series.
numbers: None recorded here.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Cross-link to subfields 01 and 02; do not repeat.

source: Gap: Schoenfeld (1985) quantitative results not verified
finding: I could not open the 1985 book or the 1992 chapter. The 60% to 20% wild goose chase figures come from Rott's quote only. Web search quota was exhausted and two public APIs returned HTTP 429 or empty results, so counts for the heuristic-training experiments (1979, 1980) are missing.
numbers: None.
limits: Missing evidence; flag for a follow-up pass or angle B.
agent_relevance: Do not cite a Schoenfeld effect size in schema notes until the original is read.

source: Gap: no LLM study found that tests Schoenfeld-style control directly
finding: The arXiv queries for Schoenfeld, working backwards and Polya returned only Llama-Polya in the time available. Most LLM work uses these heuristics under other names (least-to-most, step-back, plan-and-solve, analogical, reverse thinking).
numbers: Search limited by exhausted web-search quota and rate-limited APIs.
limits: Absence of results is not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Angle B should look for reasoning-trace episode analyses and LLM metacognition benchmarks.

source: Cross-study pattern: where each Polya heuristic helps LLMs
finding: Across the opened papers, gains are large when the failure is structural (principle recall, length generalisation, missing steps) and small on GSM8K-style arithmetic, where errors are mostly calculation.
numbers: Step-back GSM8K 84.3 vs CoT 84.4; least-to-most GSM8K +1.4; PS+ GSM8K +2.9 vs +5 or more elsewhere; Plan-and-Solve error mix 7% calculation vs 27% missing step.
limits: Different models and eras; cross-paper comparison is rough. My own synthesis.
agent_relevance: Use heuristics as gated operators, not defaults; add a calculator and a backward check for the arithmetic slice.
